observed.facings.png: Four small coupling sprites on a transparent checkerboard, lined up along the bottom of the canvas. From left to right: brass, dark gunmetal, polished aluminium with a brass ring, and grey with cyan inlays. Each is a short cylinder seen from the side. On the left is a collar with a ridged nut and a pair of claw ears above and below. On the right is a threaded stub that ends in a straight vertical edge. No dark bore is visible.
observed.south.png: A close-up of the same four couplings. Each threaded stub ends in a flat, outlined vertical cut. There is no elliptical opening or dark interior. The brass one is worn and shaded. The black one has yellow/black hazard chevrons on the collar and a bolt head. The aluminium one is bright with a brass band. The futuristic one has cyan light strips and a cyan ring port. The shading looks painterly, the outline is clean and dark, and the alpha is clean.
observed.scale.png: The four couplings beside a vanilla human on a brown ground. Each coupling is roughly a third of the pawn's width, which suits a hose fitting. They read as metal fittings, not as lumps.
observed.siblings.png: The old Coupling_Bare art in the same four looks. It is identical except that each stub ends in a 3/4 'D' face with a dark elliptical bore, so it reads as looking into the pipe opening.
observed.assembled_1.png: An offline mock in a 4x4 grid. Rows are the looks: cloth/brass, black corrugated/hazard, cloth with aluminium clamps, futuristic white/cyan spiral. Columns are N joiner, S joiner, N-pointing port coupling and S-pointing port coupling. In the joiners the coupling sits at the hose break and is drawn over the hose, at about the hose's width. In column 3 the coupling caps the top of a hose segment with its stub pointing up. In column 4 a vertical hose ends at the bottom in a coupling pointing south, beside a short horizontal hose stub. None of the south-pointing stubs show an open bore. The flat thread end reads as the end of a cylinder. A joiner seems to show one coupling shape rather than two clearly separate halves face to face, but at this size it is hard to tell.

CAMERA.seen: The card defines this sprite as lying flat and seen from straight above, rotated by C#. It is drawn as a side-on cylinder in plan, and this is consistent across all four looks and with the siblings. The 35-degree building camera does not apply to a ground-lying rotated joint sprite.

BORE.seen: Every stub ends in a flat outlined cut with threads. No elliptical dark opening appears in south.png or in any south-pointing coupling in assembled_1.png.

PORTS.seen: In the mock, each joiner coupling sits on the hose break at matching width. The port couplings sit on the hose end with the stub on the open side. This is judged from a mock, not from an in-game capture.

LAYERS.seen: The coupling draws over the hose at each join in all rows of the mock.

ROTATIONS.seen: There is one sprite, rotated by code. In the mock the N and S orientations show the same part and palette.

SIGNATURE.seen: A collar, claw ears, a ridged nut and a threaded stub with a flat cut face are all recognisable, as the description asks.

MATERIAL.seen: Worn brass, dark gunmetal, bright aluminium and grey alloy with emissive cyan all read as material with specular shading, not as flat paint.

FOOTPRINT.seen: The sprite is small, matching the 0.44-cell drawSize, and sits about at hose width in the mock. It does not overflow.

ALPHA.seen: The real alpha has been measured. The checkerboard shows through cleanly, with no halo or shadow.

OURS.seen: This is a pixel edit of the project's own shipped Coupling_Bare art.

OWNER_NOTES.seen: The owner said 'I can see into the pipe opening still'. The elliptical bore of the siblings is gone, and the south-pointing couplings in the mock show a flat threaded end.

LEGIBLE.seen: At scale.png size each still reads as a metal fitting with a distinct palette per look. It is about 14 px at 32 px/cell, which is enough for a joint marker.
